The row shows what it hosts and whether it's awake (`macOS · 6 connectors · offline`), which is exactly the row you want when the connectors it serves have all gone stale at once.
- **Connected apps** get their own labelled section below the connectors, never sorted in among them. Every other row is something your agents reach OUT to; a client reaches IN with a person's access, and no capability facet describes it.

Detail pages move to the shared connector detail route, so a device now looks like its neighbours instead of being a one-off page with its own chrome.

**Deleted:** `/connectors/runtime`, `/connectors/runtime/devices/$deviceId`, `/connectors/apps`, `devices-body.tsx`, and both user-menu dropdown items.

Revoke moves onto the client detail. It was the only consumer of `useRevokeMcpClient` in the SPA — that's what lets the apps page be deleted here rather than waiting on the Recent rebuild.

## Bugs found while building it

- **The "On device" chip could not match a device.** It resolves through `connectorIsDeviceBound()`, which tests `runtime`/`required_capability` — fields a synthesized device row has neither of. Clicking it would have listed Screen Time and Photos but not one actual device.
- **Five families of prefixed key, five hand-rolled `parse*Key` call sites**, and the route loader's prefetch guard knew about only three — firing connector-definition prefetches for keys no connector table has heard of. Replaced with one `resolveConnectorRowKind` used by the list, the detail branch, and the loader.
- **Provenance now names the host.** "Runs on a linked device. View devices" pointed at a list and left you to work out which machine.
- Clients are excluded from the facet chips, the needs-setup sort, and the empty-catalog redirect — a workspace whose only "item" is someone else's ChatGPT grant still has no connectors and belongs in the catalog.

## Scoping

Devices are user-owned and follow you across workspaces, so the list shows a device attached to this workspace **or** already serving a connection in it — "relevant here", not merely "yours". A teammate's device stays invisible; that needs an org-scoped endpoint and is deliberately out of scope.

## What

The gateway pool runs `fetch_types: false`, so postgres.js returns `text[]` columns as the raw literal `{a,b}` — a **string**. `toOAuthClient` passed those through while declaring them `string[]`, so the type lied and every consumer received a string.

## The part that isn't cosmetic

`provider.ts:567` validates redirect URIs with `client.redirect_uris.includes(redirectUri)`. On a string, `.includes()` is **substring matching, not array membership**.

For a client registered with `{https://app.example.com/callback,https://alt.example.com/cb}`, all four of these were accepted as valid redirect URIs:

```
https://app.example.com/call           (truncation)
app.example.com/callback               (scheme stripped)
com/callback,https://alt.example.com   (spans the array separator)
{https://app.example.com/callback      (includes the literal's brace)
```

`grant_types.includes('authorization_code')` at `provider.ts:122` had the same weakness.

Practical exploitability is **low** — dynamic client registration is open, so an attacker registers their own client and already controls its redirect, giving no cross-client escalation. But the check was not doing what it claimed, and the type asserted otherwise.

## Fix

One call site: `toOAuthClient`, the single read path behind both `getClient()` and `listClientsByOrganization()`. It now uses `parsePgTextArray` — a helper that **already existed** in `db/client.ts` and is used correctly in 17 other places. The boundary simply never called it.

Covers `redirect_uris`, `grant_types`, `response_types`, `contacts`.

Also fixes the web UI crash that surfaced this: `redirectUris.join(...)` threw on the new client detail view, because prod returns `"{https://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback}"`.

## Red → green

Before:
```
expect(client?.redirect_uris.includes('https://app.example.com/call')).toBe(false)
  Expected: false
  Received: true
expect(client?.grant_types?.includes('authorization_cod')).toBe(false)
  Expected: false
  Received: true
0 pass, 3 fail
```

After:
```
3 pass, 0 fail, 13 expect() calls
```

`src/auth/oauth/__tests__` + `src/lobu/__tests__`: **120 pass, 0 fail** (16 files).
`make pre-pr`: clean.

## Not fixed here

11 other ARRAY columns: `entity_ids` across five tables, `entities.enabled_classifiers`, `watchers.tags`, `watcher_versions.{recommended,required}_source_types`, `event_classifications.values`.

The codebase currently handles this three ways — parse in TS (17 sites), cast via `to_jsonb` in SQL, and raw. Closing the class means auditing each remaining site for which pattern it uses; that deserves its own PR rather than riding this one.

import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path('packages/core/src/reserved.ts'); s = p.read_text()
s = s.replace('''/**
 * Namespace prefix for a paired *device* (Mac app, Chrome extension, bridge).
 * A device is the local counterpart of a `sandbox:` row — somewhere an agent's
 * work executes — so it joins the connectors list through the same read-layer
 * union and the same detail route. The remainder is `device_workers.id`.
 */
export const DEVICE_ROW_KEY_PREFIX = "device:";

/**
 * Namespace prefix for a connected MCP *client* (ChatGPT, Claude, the CLI).
 * Unlike every other row here a client is inbound — it calls into the
 * workspace with a person's access rather than being something an agent
 * reaches out to. It shares the list and detail route so revoking a grant
 * lives next to the rest of the workspace inventory, but it is rendered in
 * its own labelled section rather than sorted in among the connectors. The
 * remainder is `oauth_clients.id` — stable and URL-safe, unlike the
 * registration group key, which embeds a client-supplied name.
 */
export const CLIENT_ROW_KEY_PREFIX = "client:";''',
'''/**
 * Path segments under `/connectors/` that are real routes, not connector keys:
 * `/connectors/device/{id}` and `/connectors/client/{id}`.
 *
 * Model providers and sandboxes are namespaced INTO the `$connectorKey` param
 * with a `prefix:` because they share that one route. Devices and clients get
 * their own static segments instead — readable URLs with no percent-encoded
 * colon — which means a connector may not claim these keys, or it would be
 * shadowed by the static route and unreachable.
 */
export const CONNECTOR_SUBROUTE_SEGMENTS = ["device", "client"] as const;

/** Whether a connector key would be shadowed by a `/connectors/*` subroute. */
export function isReservedConnectorKey(key: string): boolean {
  return (CONNECTOR_SUBROUTE_SEGMENTS as readonly string[]).includes(key);
}''')

Chrome ops: `navigate`, `evaluate`, `get_accessibility_tree`, `wait_for_selector`, `click_ref`, `type_ref`, `screenshot`, `show_notification`, `network_intercept_*`, `close_tab`.
92:- Per-call dispatch latency is 5–60s and virtualized lists recycle content out — for paginated scrapes, iterate inside the connector's own run, not via one-shot `evaluate`s.
93:- **Connector-side changes ship via re-apply, not the app release.** Per-org connectors (`examples/personal-agent`) live in `connector_definitions`/`connector_versions` and only update on `lobu apply` (or `connections.installConnector` for a single bundle). An app deploy that adds a *capability* (e.g. `show_notification`) does nothing until the connector that *calls* it is re-applied. **And a new chrome action also needs the matching handler in the extension build** — dispatching `show_notification` to an older installed extension fails with `Owletto for Chrome: unknown dispatch ... action_key='show_notification'`. So three things gate such a notification: an up-to-date extension build (the handler), a re-applied connector (the call), and macOS notification permission on the extension.

## Grab the secret + session token

```bash
# Local dev backend uses .env's BETTER_AUTH_SECRET
SECRET=$(grep '^BETTER_AUTH_SECRET=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)

# Prod uses the secret on the K8s pod
SECRET=$(kubectl exec -n summaries-prod \
  $(kubectl get pod -n summaries-prod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=lobu-app -o name | head -1 | sed 's|pod/||') \
  -- printenv BETTER_AUTH_SECRET)

# Session token from the DB (prod DB serves both targets)
DB="$(grep '^DATABASE_URL=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)"
TOKEN=$(psql "$DB" -tAc "SELECT token FROM session WHERE \"userId\" = '<user_id>' AND \"expiresAt\" > NOW() ORDER BY \"updatedAt\" DESC LIMIT 1")
```

## Sign the cookie

better-auth uses HMAC-SHA256, base64, then URL-encode — base64**url** does *not* validate.

```bash
SIGNED=$(SECRET="$SECRET" TOKEN="$TOKEN" node -e '
  const {createHmac}=require("node:crypto");
  const sig=createHmac("sha256",process.env.SECRET).update(process.env.TOKEN).digest("base64");
  console.log(encodeURIComponent(`${process.env.TOKEN}.${sig}`));
')
```

Cookie name is `__Secure-better-auth.session_token` whenever the baseURL is `https://` (prod and Tailscale dev qualify; only plain-http localhost uses the unprefixed `better-auth.session_token`).

## Drive the browser

```bash
agent-browser --session lobu-verify open "https://app.lobu.ai/"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify eval "document.cookie='__Secure-better-auth.session_token=$SIGNED; path=/; secure; samesite=lax'"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify open "https://app.lobu.ai/<path>"
agent-browser --session lobu-verify wait --text "<expected text>" --timeout 25000
agent-browser --session lobu-verify snapshot -i      # find @refs

## What

Devices and MCP clients each had their own page, reachable **only** from the user dropdown at the bottom of the sidebar — workspace plumbing filed under account settings. Nothing on the Connectors page linked to either.

Both now live on `/connectors`, in one list:

- **Devices** join the main list under the Runtime facet, synthesized the same way sandboxes and model providers already are. A paired Mac is the local counterpart of a remote sandbox — somewhere an agent's work runs. The row says what it hosts and whether it's awake (`macOS · 6 connectors · offline`).
- **Connected apps** are ordinary rows in that same list, not a second bordered box with its own heading and paragraph. Only LIVE grants: `connected` means an unexpired token, and prod carries twelve dead registrations against two live ones — listing them all buried the connectors under a wall of revoked apps. The dead ones stay on the MCP client page.
- **The first-party apps become static entries.** Owletto for Mac, Owletto for Chrome, the CLI, an MCP client and the self-hosted bridge each get an instruction page at `/connectors/app/{id}` that also lists what connected through it. An entry drops off the connectors list once it has paired a device, and stays in the Add catalog for the next machine.

Detail pages use the shared connector chrome (`ConnectorPageShell` + `DetailHeader` + `PageSection`), and devices and clients route on real segments — `/connectors/device/{id}`, `/connectors/client/{id}` — instead of a percent-encoded `device%3A…` key.

**Deleted:** `/connectors/runtime`, `/connectors/runtime/devices/$deviceId`, `/connectors/apps`, `devices-body.tsx`, both user-menu dropdown items, and — once the Devices page went — `device-connect.tsx` and its only consumer `command-popover.tsx`. Its content is what the app catalog is built from.

**Filter chips are capability-only.** OAuth / API key / App install are gone: how a connector authenticates is a detail of setting up the one you already picked, and the chips overlapped Data almost exactly.

## Bugs found while building it

- **The "On device" chip could not match a device.** It resolves through `connectorIsDeviceBound()`, which tests `runtime`/`required_capability` — fields a synthesized device row has neither of. Clicking it would have listed Screen Time and Photos but not one actual device. Now an explicit `isDevice` flag, because the row key stopped being routable.
- **Five families of prefixed key, five hand-rolled `parse*Key` call sites**, and the route loader's prefetch guard knew about only three — firing connector-definition prefetches for keys no connector table has heard of. Replaced with one `resolveConnectorRowKind`, down to three kinds once devices and clients got real routes.
- **Client rows linked to a connector key that no table has.** `client-row:{id}` went to `$connectorKey` and would have landed on connector-not-found.
- **Provenance now names the host.** "Runs on a linked device. View devices" pointed at a list and left you to work out which machine.

## Scoping

Devices are user-owned and follow you across workspaces, so the list shows a device attached to this workspace **or** already serving a connection in it — "relevant here", not merely "yours". A teammate's device stays invisible; that needs an org-scoped endpoint and is out of scope.

## Verified

**1134/1134 tests pass** (`vitest run`), `tsc -b` clean, biome clean on every changed file. The route smoke test's coverage guard caught the stale `ROUTES` entries when routes were deleted and the missing ones when `device`/`client`/`app` were added — all three now have cases.

Booted against the prod API and clicked through every surface: [screenshot tour](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/015b124a-e4ee-49ea-8c56-f04373c11638). After-only — the browser session's prod cookie expired mid-session and could not be re-minted without the prod database URL.

## Pairs with

- lobu-ai/lobu#2380 — registered name over driver (this PR drops `firstParty` and binds `drivenBy`)
- lobu-ai/lobu#2381 — `oauth_clients` array parsing, which fixed a `redirectUris.join` crash on the client detail
- The follow-up lobu PR reserves `device` / `client` / `app` (and `create` / `deployments`) as connector keys, so an installed connector can never shadow one of these routes.
EOF

content.text:
Both changes are in and the review is posted. Here's where it landed.

## The four things you raised

**Actions stays, auth chips go.** The chip row is capability-only now: All / Data / Chat / Actions / Inference / Runtime / On device. OAuth, API key and App install were one class, not two — how a connector authenticates is a detail of setting up the one you already picked, and they overlapped Data almost exactly. I removed all three rather than the two you named, since leaving App install behind would just be the next instance of the same thing.

**Connected apps are ordinary rows.** No second bordered box, no heading, no paragraph. Building it surfaced something worth knowing: `connected` means the client still holds an unexpired token, and your workspace has **twelve dead registrations against two live ones**. Folded in flat, the connectors vanished under a wall of revoked apps. So the list carries live grants only, and the dead ones live on the MCP client page — which is the honest split, since a revoked grant is history rather than inventory.

**CLI and MCP client are static entries.** Along with Owletto for Mac, Owletto for Chrome, and the self-hosted bridge. Each has a real page at `/connectors/app/{id}` — instructions first, then what connected through it. The Mac page lists your two Macs; the MCP client page lists all 18 apps, live first. An entry drops off the list once it has paired something (which is why you only see CLI and MCP client — your Mac and Chrome are already in), and stays in the catalog for the next machine.

**The add page:** no, it showed none of them. It does now — all five, beside the connectors, providers and sandbox kinds.

Cleanup is done. Final state:

## Merged

- **owletto#663** → `3d4c0465` — the connectors surface
- **lobu#2386** → `11facd36` — route-segment reservation + pointer bump. All required checks green (unit, integration, typecheck, frontend, migrations, format-lint, base-branch-guard, pi-review).

## Cleaned up

Three worktrees removed — `mcp-client-identity`, `pg-array-boundary`, `connect-merge`. `make task-clean` refused all three first, claiming unpushed commits; that's the squash-merge ancestry trap, not lost work. I verified before forcing by diffing each branch against `origin/main` scoped to the files it actually touched — all three empty, so every line is on main.

Dropping `lobu_feat_mcp_client_identity` took the four seeded `mcp_client_devseed_*` rows and their tokens with it. Dev servers on 5180/5273/9198 stopped, `/tmp/pat.txt` and `/tmp/clients.json` gone, worktree list pruned, main checkout clean.

**One thing I could not do:** revoke the prod PAT `owl_pat_K46U1zQ…` and the `devseed-verify` PAT. `lobu token revoke` writes to `public.revoked_tokens` and needs `DATABASE_URL` pointed at prod, which no `.env` in this checkout has. That's yours to run from an environment that has it — or say the word and I'll look for a route that goes through the API instead.

---

**Confidence: high (92)** that both PRs are merged and the worktree work is fully on main — verified by scoped diff against `origin/main`, not by the branch-ahead count that misled `task-clean`. **High (88)** on the UI, from clicking through all four surfaces against the prod API before merge.

Next, in the order I'd take them:

1. **Prod-verify after rollout** — #2380 (client names read as registered, not `claude-code`), #2381 (client detail loads without the `redirectUris.join` crash), #2386 (the new connectors list, app pages, and clean `/connectors/device/{id}` URLs). I can set a self-rescheduling wakeup gated on the deployed SHA.
2. **Revoke those two PATs** once you have a prod `DATABASE_URL` to hand.
3. **Exercise what I didn't** — the copy button on the app pages, and Revoke on the client detail.
4. **The "Chrome appears twice" unnamed-device issue** — still open, and now more visible with devices on the main list.
